what_it_does: When multiple processors (CPUs and GPUs) share a system, they each have small fast private caches (memory close to the chip) and must coordinate so that a value written by one processor is visible to others in the right order — this coordination is called cache coherence. A common approach called 'write-through with release consistency' has a processor that finishes writing send those writes to a central directory (a record-keeper for which processor holds which data) and then wait for the directory to confirm the correct order before the next processor can read. This round-trip communication adds latency and extra traffic on the links between chips. CORD moves the ordering responsibility to the directory itself: the directory collects incoming writes, enforces the required ordering locally, and notifies other processors when it is safe to read — eliminating the round-trip from the writing processor. Compact metadata in the directory tracks which writes are still in-flight, keeping the storage overhead small while scaling to multiple directories.
